title: Teaching Harry Carney breathing and low notes
summary: Waters describes teaching Carney correct breathing, vibrato and the 'Doo' rather than 'Too' attack for low notes, and credits this for Carney's big baritone sound.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Right. And Carney found you and he studied with you. Can you mention anything about it? What was it like, what was he like? How young was he?
Well, he was, he couldn't play saxophone, he was just learning then.
I don't know, I didn't bother with clarinet, his clarinet at all.
So he came to you as -
What had been his instrument at the Conservatory?
Well then, he had played saxophone before, he wasn't a beginning student.

Well, I would say beginner, see, because I mean, when I took him, things that he didn't know, how to breath correct, he didn't - and he, and his little tone was straight, because that's all they knew, see. Have you ever heard virtuoso saxophonists play? Have you ever heard a guy like Rudy Wiedoft?

Yeah, well yeah, and have you ever heard another guy named Benny H-, no, I think that's from Philadelphia. Well, those guys mostly - there's one in Paris right now by the name Mule, got the same thing. They get a straight tone, that's where some of the smartest stuff is coming in with the straight tone, which sounds so bad sometimes. But no vibrato, no coloring a note, just a 'Dooooo' - 'cause they didn't know how to

play that saxophone, that's like when it's a new instrument. It's clarinet that people raise hell with, but not the saxophone. And so Carney, as he told me, the reason that he wanted to make a change from the Conservatory, because he didn't - he would listen to other guys play in the dance bands and so forth with that very beautiful sound, you know, see, and he didn't have it. See what I mean? So he wanted to come, he wanted to know how to get that vibrato, that's what I taught him and how to breath, how to make low notes. As far as the book's concerned, he could play those exercises, understand what I mean? But the technical part of playin' the saxophone and gettin' the sound, that's what I, the way I came in, understand what I mean? That's why I say he was a beginner in that category, understand what I mean? But he could play, he could play the books, he could play his exercises. But he couldn't breath, he didn't breath right. There's a way of breathing that saves your health, if you don't know that you can hurt your throat, you can - a whole lot of things if you don't breathe correct, you know. For instance, if you - I taught him this, hold your hand over, I'll show you what I mean. I taught him this, I taught him this - like (demonstrates breathing with PS holding his hand over BW's stomach) - See that? Now here's what can be wrong. (demonstrates incorrect breathing) See the difference? - well that's what I taught him, how to breath. And also, and now I told him how to make low notes, which is the certain way to make low notes on the saxophone. I mean to verify that, that's why you hear so much high saxophone playing, particular tenors. It's not that they are trying to play high, it's just (laughs) they can't play low, 'cause there's a lot of complications in it. For instance, you got to get the right mouthpiece, then your horn got to be in condition. Then you got to know how to make a low note, see what I mean? So it took Carney, it took Carney two weeks - or rather, say two lessons, rather - to learn how to make D on the saxophone right off without slurring to it, to say "Doo". You know why? - because they was teachin' him how to say, instead of saying "Doo", they were teachin' "Too". Because that's one of the first things you learned, the "Too", "Too", "Too", "Too", "Too", "Too", see? But more advanced studies is not to make, say - like I'm playin' on, like when we play ballads, like I play ballads and so forth. You don't ever strike a low note with "Too" because they, anything could start to happen. You strike it with "Doo" and not "Too" at all. See, little things like that, that's what I taught Carney. And that's what I used - and that's why I play in the low part of my horn, as you noticed, you know what I mean? You notice I play in the low, I make the notes - I can play a whole chorus and don't even use the octave key, see what I mean? And that's what I taught Carney to do, that's why he excelled in baritone, 'cause for a baritone you've got to play. That's what, that's the character of his playing from Gerry Mulligan, and they both were great. If you notice Carney's sound is bigger because he plays lower - well, I give myself the credit because I know how long it took him to do that, to take, pick up the - 'cause I had him pick up the saxophone like this. I said to him "Make this D in the first added space below the staff, right off without any other sound". See, so he said "Too" and everything come out, instead of D coming out the A came up, you know, fourth line, octave above. Because he's usin' the wrong syllable, you see what I mean? So I said "Look, then you say you", I say "Get your mouth in position and don't squeeze too much, just say "Doo", 'Doo'. Not 'Duh' like that, it would force - 'Doo', 'Doo'". Finally he got it, and that's the key of playing in the low part of a saxophone, which is stuff that many saxophone players don't know even today. That's why you hear 'em play, I

mean, that's why they can't get those low notes, listen to it. I'm not, of course I'm more advanced now, like I take, I can do it, Buddy Tate can, Coleman could, naturally because he's the father of all that stuff, see. Guys like Don Byas were perfect on it, Charlie Ventura mastered it, I know many. But I mean, that's where the secret is, you have to know how to do it, and that's what he was payin' for. Understand what I mean?
